title: Setting up and running a Cassandra cluster
goal: By the end, you can set up a Cassandra node from its folders and the few settings that matter, add and remove nodes and say which data moves where, keep a cluster healthy with repair, careful restarts and snapshots, add a second datacenter, and say what Cassandra 6.0 changes about how the ring is kept.
opening:
Picture an office like the one in the last lesson, with three clerks, each with a full copy of the account files. For the busy season, a fourth clerk is hired. She takes over a share of the alphabet and copies those files from the colleagues handing them over. Soon the office runs out of cabinet space. Nobody told the old clerks to shred the files they gave away, so many files now exist four times instead of three.

Cassandra behaves the same way. When a new machine joins, the old ones keep every row they handed over, until someone runs one command. It's easy to assume a database tidies up after itself, because the join ends with a log line saying the new node is NORMAL, which sounds like the end.

In Inside a Cassandra cluster, we watched a running cluster keep its map. In this lesson, we'll set up a node, add and remove one, keep the copies equal, take a backup and add a second datacenter. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A fourth node joins a Cassandra cluster of three nodes that keeps three copies of every row. It copies its share of the data and shows UN, up and normal. What do the three old nodes do with the rows they no longer need to keep?
options: Delete them as soon as the copying finishes
Keep them until someone runs `nodetool cleanup` on each old node
Drop them the next time they tidy their files in the background
Move them into a folder kept for the new node
warmup.why: Cassandra never deletes data because ownership moved, and its routine background tidying, compaction, keeps every row it finds. In the Try it, the old nodes still held all 5,000 partitions after the join. `nodetool cleanup`, a special compaction, cut cass1 to 3,729. The first option is the trap: the join's last log line says NORMAL, which sounds like the end. The folder in the last option exists, but it's for hints, writes a down node missed.

sections.h: A node is one Java program, four folders and two settings files
sections.body:
This lesson builds a Cassandra cluster and runs it, with three ideas from earlier lessons: the ring of 16 tokens per node, rebalancing when nodes come and go, and the hints and repair that keep copies equal.

A Cassandra node is one Java program, `org.apache.cassandra.service.CassandraDaemon`, plus the files it owns. An operator, the person who runs the cluster, works with those files and with the few settings that tie one node to the others.

You install two things: a JDK, the kit that runs Java programs, and Cassandra. As of November 2026 the latest stable release is 5.0.9, from August 2026, and the labs pin it. 6.0 is an alpha, an early test version. The 5.0 docs ask for Java 11 or 17, and the `cassandra:5.0.9` image ships 17. In the lab's Docker image, `/etc/cassandra` holds the settings, `/var/lib/cassandra` the data and `/var/log/cassandra` the logs.

The data folder has four parts, and each one is a mechanism you've met:

- `commitlog/` holds the commit log, the file every change is added to first so a crash loses nothing (Wide-column stores with Cassandra). It comes in 32 MiB pieces, reused once their writes are saved in table files.
- `data/` has one folder per keyspace, a group of tables that share one replication setting, and inside it one per table, such as `payments/ledger-a0d7ae60...`. Those hold the SSTables, the sorted files where a table's rows live on disk. `snapshots/` and `backups/` appear in there later.
- `hints/` keeps writes for replicas, the nodes holding a row's copies, while they're down, one file per node.
- `saved_caches/` holds the key cache, a note of where recently read rows sit in the files, saved every 4 hours so a restarted node doesn't start cold.

Memory has two users. One is the heap, the memory the JVM (the program that runs Java code) manages for Cassandra's objects. The other is the operating system's page cache, its copy of recently read file data in RAM (The page cache, writeback and fsync), which serves SSTable reads. If you don't set the heap, a start script, `cassandra-env.sh`, takes half the machine's RAM, up to 31 GB. Inside a container that rule misfires. The script asks the `free` command how much memory there is, and `free` reports the 7.75 GB of the virtual machine Docker runs everything in, not the container's 1 GB limit (Containers are processes: namespaces and cgroups explains why). The lab nodes get `-Xmx320M`, a 320 MB heap, only because the Compose file, the lab's list of containers and their settings, sets `MAX_HEAP_SIZE`. A node that goes over its container's limit is killed by the kernel, the core of the operating system, and exits with code 137.

**Set the heap yourself, and leave the rest of the RAM to the page cache.**

Files are half of a node. Next, we'll read the settings that join three of them into one cluster.

sections.h: cassandra.yaml: the questions a node answers before it can join
sections.body:
The `cassandra.yaml` in the 5.0.9 image has 2,485 lines, and almost all of them can stay as they are. A new node has to answer a handful of questions before it can join a cluster, and each answer is a setting.

Which cluster is this? `cluster_name`. Gossip, the once-a-second exchange that keeps every node's map in step, drops every message from a node with a different name (the receiver logs `ClusterName mismatch`), so a test node pointed at the real cluster by mistake can't join it.

Whom do I ask first? `seeds`, under `seed_provider`: two or three steady nodes per datacenter, the same list on every node, and never a node joining for the first time (Inside a Cassandra cluster explained why).

Which address? `listen_address` is the one other nodes connect to, on port 7000 (a port is the number that says which program on a machine a message is for), and `rpc_address`, on port 9042, is for clients. The file warns that a `listen_address` of 0.0.0.0, meaning every address the machine has, "is always wrong". `rpc_address` may be 0.0.0.0 if `broadcast_rpc_address` tells drivers, the libraries apps use to talk to Cassandra, the real one.

Where am I? The snitch, the part that knows each node's datacenter and rack: `endpoint_snitch: GossipingPropertyFileSnitch`, plus `dc=` and `rack=` in `cassandra-rackdc.properties`. The default, `SimpleSnitch`, puts every node in `datacenter1` and `rack1`, and the production docs say changing racks after setup isn't supported.

How many tokens? `num_tokens: 16`, with `allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor` set to your number of copies. Both apply only at a node's first start. The production docs suggest 4 tokens for clusters expected to grow past 30 nodes, and advise against 16 above 50.

How safe is a confirmed write on one node? `commitlog_sync: periodic` with `commitlog_sync_period: 10000ms`. The node confirms a write before it forces the commit log onto the disk (an fsync), and fsyncs every 10 seconds, so a power cut on one machine can lose its last 10 seconds of writes. The other replicas still have them, which is one more reason three copies aren't optional.

Last, keyspaces. `CREATE KEYSPACE payments WITH replication = {'class': 'NetworkTopologyStrategy', 'dc1': 3}` names a datacenter, and the name must match what the snitch reports, letter for letter. The docs say production clusters should never use `SimpleStrategy`, the rule that ignores datacenters and racks, and that includes Cassandra's own system keyspaces. `describecluster` shows `system_auth`, which holds users and passwords, on `SimpleStrategy` with one copy. Losing one node can then lock everyone out once logins are switched on. Change it to NetworkTopologyStrategy with 3 copies per datacenter, then repair it.

With these right, the cluster is ready to grow. Next, we'll add a fourth node and watch exactly what moves.

sections.h: Adding and removing a node: which data moves, and from where
sections.body:
When cass4 joined the lab cluster, it received 276, 300 and 280 KiB from the three old nodes, and none of them deleted anything. Adding a node is the slowest routine job in Cassandra, because data has to stream, be copied over the network, before the new node can serve it. Its 16 new tokens cut slices off existing ranges, the stretches of the ring between tokens, so it takes a little from every node. And nothing moves until an operator starts a node or runs a command, so a node that's down for an hour never triggers a move.

1. cass4 starts with the same `cluster_name` and seeds, empty data folders, and its own address not in the seed list, so it will bootstrap, the first-start step that copies its share of the data.
2. It learns the map from a seed and waits until it has the schema (`JOINING: waiting for ring information`, then `schema complete, ready to bootstrap`).
3. It picks 16 tokens with the allocator and announces them in gossip with a BOOT status. The others now show it as `UJ`, up and joining. From this moment, coordinators (the nodes that take requests and pass them on) send cass4 a copy of every new write for the ranges it's about to own, so nothing written during the copy is missed.
4. It sleeps `ring_delay`, 30 seconds, so the whole cluster has heard.
5. It streams. With 16 tokens and three copies, cass4 becomes a replica of 47 ranges, and it takes each range from the replica it replaces: the node that held that range before and won't afterwards. Cassandra insists on that source (`cassandra.consistent.rangemovement`, true by default), so the three new copies hold exactly what the three old ones held. Copying from another replica could lose a write: one confirmed only by the replaced node and one other would end up on a single node, and two majorities would no longer be sure to share a node. The lab checks its model against cass4's log of all 47.
6. It switches to NORMAL and shows `UN`.

That took 90 seconds here; real nodes take hours, and the worked example sizes one. Join one node at a time and wait for `UN`, because two joins at once would each work out their ranges against a ring that's about to change.

The old nodes keep everything, like the clerks who never shred until told. Cassandra doesn't delete data for ranges a node no longer owns, so their Load, the data each one stores, stayed at 1.16 MiB. `nodetool cleanup` on each old node rewrites its SSTables without those ranges: cass1 went from 5,000 partitions, groups of rows that share a key, to 3,729. Run it on every old node after the last new node has joined, one at a time, because it's a compaction, a rewrite of the node's files, and costs disk work. The office picture breaks here: a clerk would notice the extra files, and a node never does.

Removing a node is a join in reverse. `nodetool decommission`, run on the node that leaves, marks it LEAVING, streams its ranges and hints to the new owners, and leaves: cass4 sent 7 SSTables to each of the three. A dead node can't stream, so `nodetool removenode` makes the survivors stream for it, and the compare box below sets the two side by side.

Steps 2 to 4 lean on gossip: cass4 sleeps 30 seconds, hoping every node has heard. Cassandra 6.0, in alpha since April 2026, replaces the hope with a log. Its Transactional Cluster Metadata turns membership, token ownership and schema into entries of one log, which a Cluster Metadata Service (CMS) on a few nodes orders by consensus, a vote in which a majority must agree. Every node applies the entries in order of their epoch numbers. Before each next step of a join, the joining node waits until the others confirm the last epoch, a progress barrier. Here a second 6.0-alpha2 node joins a one-node cluster (log trimmed):

```text
Committing REGISTER
Committing PREPARE_JOIN
Committing START_JOIN
Collected acknowledgements from [/172.24.0.2:7000, /172.24.0.3:7000] ... progress barrier for epoch Epoch{epoch=6} at EACH_QUORUM
Committing MID_JOIN
Collected acknowledgements from [/172.24.0.2:7000, /172.24.0.3:7000] ... progress barrier for epoch Epoch{epoch=7} at EACH_QUORUM
Committing FINISH_JOIN
NORMAL
```

No 30-second sleep: the join took half a second, and the log then held those steps as epochs 4 to 8.

Next, we'll keep the copies equal from day to day.

try.title: Add cass4, clean up, then decommission it
steps: Give the cluster something to move: 50,000 ledger rows (about a minute), then flush every node, writing its memory to SSTables, so `nodetool status` counts the data as Load. The load may print a `WriteTimeout ... will retry later` or two on a busy laptop; it retries them. Check `nodetool status payments`: every node owns 100%.

Start cass4, which the Compose file keeps behind a profile, an optional group of containers: `docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml --profile grow up -d cass4`. Run `nodetool status payments` on cass1 every 20 seconds or so. Predict the letters cass4 shows, then its Owns, and whether the old nodes' Load changes. When cass4 is `UN`, read its log.
Run `nodetool cleanup payments` on cass1, cass2 and cass3, one after the other, and compare the partition counts before and after. Wait a minute and check the Load column again: it travels by gossip.

Decommission cass4 (about 70 seconds), read its log, check `nodetool status`, then remove the container: `docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml --profile grow rm -sfv cass4`. Leave the three nodes running for the next Try it.

Optional, about 2 GB and two minutes: start one Cassandra 6.0-alpha2 node with `docker compose -f env/cassandra6.yml up -d --wait` (the Transactions track uses the same file), print its Cluster Metadata Service and its metadata log, then stop it with `docker compose -f env/cassandra6.yml down -v`.

sections.h: Keeping it healthy: checks, repair, restarts and snapshots
sections.body:
`nodetool` is how an operator talks to a node. It reaches the node through JMX, Java's built-in way to manage a running program from outside, and by default a node accepts JMX only from its own machine, on port 7199. Five commands cover most days:

- `status`: `UN` everywhere, or a `DN` (down), `UJ` or `UL` (leaving) that shouldn't be there?
- `describecluster`: one schema version, so every node has the same table definitions?
- `tablestats <keyspace.table>`: the SSTable count, read and write times, `Maximum tombstones per slice` and `Compacted partition maximum bytes`. A tombstone is the marker Cassandra writes for a delete (Wide-column stores with Cassandra), and the largest partition should stay under the 100 MB guideline.
- `compactionstats`: waiting compactions, the background work that merges SSTables. A growing number means compaction is falling behind, and reads slow down as SSTables pile up.
- `tpstats`: waiting and blocked work per thread pool, a group of threads that does one kind of work, and dropped messages, writes a node gave up on because they waited too long.

Repair is the one job Cassandra never starts by itself, and it has a deadline. Hints cover 3 hours of downtime, and read repair covers the keys someone reads. Everything else drifts until `nodetool repair` compares the copies range by range, using Merkle trees, trees of hashes that let two nodes find the ranges that differ without sending all the data (the Replication track's anti-entropy). Deletes make it urgent. A replica that misses a tombstone for longer than `gc_grace_seconds`, 10 days by default, can bring the deleted row back, because the other copies may have thrown the tombstone away by then.

Plain `nodetool repair` is incremental: it compares only data written since the last one. `--full` compares everything. The docs suggest incremental every 1 to 3 days and full every 1 to 3 weeks, and at the very least every node within 7 days while `gc_grace_seconds` is 10 days. A run repairs every range the node holds, so running it on all nodes repairs each range three times; `-pr` limits each run to the node's primary ranges, those it holds as the first copy, and then you run it on every node. `--preview` shows what would stream, without streaming.

Restart one node at a time, and drain it first. `nodetool drain` stops client traffic, announces the shutdown in gossip (so peers mark the node down at once, instead of waiting 20 seconds for their suspicion score, phi, to climb), and flushes every memtable, the table kept in memory, to an SSTable. The restart then has nothing to replay: `Log replay complete, 0 replayed mutations in 68 ms`. A rolling restart is drain, restart, wait for `UN`, then the next node. With three copies and `QUORUM`, a majority of them, one node down at a time never blocks a range.

Backups start with `nodetool snapshot`. It flushes and hard-links every SSTable of the keyspace into `snapshots/<tag>/`, next to a `schema.cql` that recreates the table. A hard link is a second name for the same file on disk (File systems: inodes, links and file descriptors). So a snapshot takes no time and no extra space, until compaction deletes the originals, which the snapshot then keeps alive. `incremental_backups: true`, or `nodetool enablebackup`, hard-links every newly written SSTable into `backups/`. Neither is a backup until it's copied off the node, and after that, clear it (`nodetool clearsnapshot`) or it fills the disk.

**Repair, drain and backups happen only if someone schedules them. Schedule them.**

Next, we'll give the cluster a second home.

Turn on incremental backups, write a row, flush, and look in `backups/`. Clean up afterwards: `nodetool clearsnapshot -t before-upgrade payments` and `nodetool disablebackup`.

sections.h: A second datacenter, and a checklist for a real cluster
sections.body:
In the Try it, a read in a new datacenter returned 0 rows for a ledger entry that existed. The keyspace already said `'dc2': 1`, but nobody had copied the data to dc2 yet. That gap is the hard part of adding a datacenter.

A second datacenter is for a region going dark, for users far from the first one, or for analytics, big reports over all the data, kept off the payment nodes. Each datacenter holds full copies with its own replication factor, and clients stay local. `LOCAL_QUORUM` waits for a majority in the coordinator's own datacenter only, so a round trip to another region, about 70 ms, never sits in the path of a write. The other datacenter still gets every write, in the background.

The steps, as the Try it ran them:

1. Start the new nodes with `dc=dc2`, the same cluster name and seeds, and `auto_bootstrap: false`, so they join the ring without streaming. They own 0% of `payments`.
2. `ALTER KEYSPACE payments` to add `'dc2'` (3 in production), and do the same for `system_auth`, `system_distributed` and `system_traces`.
3. On each new node, `nodetool rebuild -- dc1` streams that node's share from dc1: about 1.2 MiB from three nodes here.
4. Only then send that region's clients to dc2, with the setting `basic.load-balancing-policy.local-datacenter = dc2` in the Java driver, the library Java apps use.

Leave `auto_bootstrap` at its default, and the new node streams some ranges as it joins, after which `rebuild` refuses with `Discovered existing bootstrap data ...; aborting bootstrap`.

Most of a checklist for a real cluster is decided before the first node starts, because the cluster name, tokens, snitch and racks can't be changed in place later. The rest is routine that has to happen on a calendar, or it doesn't happen at all.

| Area | Do this | Because |
|---|---|---|
| Racks | 3 per datacenter (one per availability zone, a separate building of a cloud region), equal in size | one copy per rack; a small rack's nodes carry more |
| Before the first start | `cluster_name`, the snitch, `dc` and `rack`, `num_tokens` (16, or 4 past about 30 nodes), the allocator | none of these can change in place |
| Seeds | 2 or 3 per datacenter, one list everywhere, never a joining node | a seed never bootstraps |
| Keyspaces | NetworkTopologyStrategy, 3 copies per datacenter, system keyspaces too | `system_auth` starts with one copy |
| Clients | `LOCAL_QUORUM`, the driver's local datacenter set | no wait across regions |
| Memory | `MAX_HEAP_SIZE` set by hand | the default reads the host's RAM |
| Time | NTP, a service that keeps clocks in step, everywhere | the newest timestamp wins a conflict |
| Security | logins, permissions and TLS (encrypted connections) from day one | the defaults let anyone in |
| Changes | one node at a time; cleanup after adding; drain before restarting | ranges move against a ring that holds still |
| Repair | every node within `gc_grace_seconds` | deleted rows come back after 10 days |
| Backups | copied off the node, cleared after, restores tested | a hard link dies with its disk |
| Monitoring | node states, dropped messages, waiting compactions, hints, p99 latency (the time 99 requests in 100 beat) | they move before users notice |

That's the limit of running Cassandra 5.0: every row is a step a person has to remember, in order, one node at a time.

compare.title: Taking a node out: decommission or removenode

a.label: nodetool decommission (the node is alive)
a.src:
# run ON the node that leaves
nodetool decommission

# LEAVING: sleeping 30000 ms ...
# LEAVING: streaming data to other nodes   <- it sends its own data
# LEAVING: streaming hints to other nodes
# Announcing that I have left the ring
# DECOMMISSIONED

b.label: nodetool removenode (the node is dead)
b.src:
# run on ANY live node, with the dead node's host ID
nodetool status        # DN  ...  3af36864-e701-...
nodetool removenode 3af36864-e701-442b-862a-96cb9bb04775
nodetool removenode status

# the surviving replicas stream to the new owners;
# the dead node's copy is gone

compare.note: Both end with the node's tokens off the ring and its ranges owned by others. Decommission is the clean path: the leaving node sends exactly what it held, including its hints, while it's still a full replica. Removenode is for a node that can't take part, so the data comes from the other replicas, and anything only the dead node had (a write confirmed by it alone at ONE, a hint it was holding) is lost unless repair finds it elsewhere. Removenode takes the dead node's host ID, its unique name from `nodetool status`, and if the node was down longer than `max_hint_window`, 3 hours, repair afterwards. If a new machine is taking the dead one's place, `-Dcassandra.replace_address_first_boot=<dead address>` is better than either: the new node takes the dead one's tokens, and nobody else's ranges move.

worked.title: Plan growing a six-node payments cluster to nine

steps.say: Write down what you have and what the new layout will be. Grow every rack by one node, so the racks stay equal.
steps.code:
now     6 nodes, RF 3, racks a/b/c with 2 nodes each, 600 GB per node
after   9 nodes, racks a/b/c with 3 nodes each
per node after: 600 GB x 6 / 9 = 400 GB

steps.say: Estimate the copy for one new node. Each sender is slowed to `stream_throughput_outbound`, 24 MiB/s by default, and a new node receives from several senders at once.
steps.code:
data to receive     about 400 GB
sources             about 3, at 24 MiB/s each = 72 MiB/s
time                400 x 1024 MiB / 72 MiB/s = 5,689 s, about 1.6 h
three nodes, one at a time: about 5 h

steps.say: Add them one at a time, one per rack, and check each before the next. Don't clean up in between, because the next join moves ranges again.
steps.code:
for each new node (rack a, then b, then c):
  start it (not in its own seed list, same cluster_name, its rack in rackdc)
  nodetool status          # UJ ... then UN
  nodetool netstats        # streams finished, nothing pending

steps.say: Clean up the six old nodes. Cleanup is a compaction that rewrites everything the node holds, limited to `compaction_throughput`, 64 MiB/s in 5.0.9's settings file.
steps.code:

after          Load about 400 GB, Owns about 33.3% on all nine

nodetool describecluster    # one schema version

lab.title: Model token-range movement and check it against the real cluster
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. They need no Docker: they read `nodetool ring`, `describering` and cass4's stream log, captured from the Try it and kept in `src/test/resources/sfz/shard/l06/`. Five of eight fail with `NotImplementedError`. The three that pass check the given `Ring` against the real cluster: its walk over replicas matches `describering` range by range, and its `owns` matches the Owns column of `nodetool status`.

Write `bootstrapSources`: for each range cass4 holds after the join, its old replicas, its new replicas, and the one old replica that isn't a new one. Two tests pass, including the one that compares you with the 47 `Bootstrap: range ... exists on ...` lines cass4 logged.
Write `cleanup`: for each range of the new ring, the old replicas that aren't replicas any more. The test checks that each old node deletes exactly what it streamed away.
Write `decommissionTargets`: for each range the leaving node holds, the replica that appears once it's gone. All eight pass, including the one that hands every range back to the node it came from.

Experiment: in `bootstrapSources`, stream every range from the first old replica (the primary) instead. The test against the real log fails, because Cassandra picks the replica being replaced, not the first one. Put it back.
hints: Every range of the new ring sits inside exactly one range of the old ring, because the old tokens are a subset of the new ones. So `before.replicasOf(range.end)` gives the old replicas of a new range.
`old - new.toSet()` keeps the order of `old`. With RF 3 and three old nodes it has exactly one element; `.singleOrNull() ?: old.first()` covers small clusters.
`getOrPut(node) { linkedSetOf() } += range` builds a map of sets in one line, and `sortedMapOf` keeps the output stable.
For decommission, compare `ring.replicas(range)` with `ring.withoutNode(leaving).replicasOf(range.end)`; the new name in the second list receives the range.

drill.title: The node-change runbook, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the commands, in order, to (1) add cass4 to a three-node cluster with three copies, (2) later retire cass2, which is healthy, and (3) deal with cass3, whose disk died and won't come back. After each command, write what you check before going on.

answer.src:
# 1. add cass4: same cluster_name and seeds, not its own seed, empty data dirs
start cass4
nodetool status                  # UJ, then UN; Owns about 75% each
nodetool cleanup                 # on cass1, cass2, cass3, one at a time
nodetool tablestats ...          # partitions and Load drop to about 75%

# 2. retire cass2 (alive): it streams its own ranges away
nodetool decommission            # run ON cass2
nodetool status                  # cass2 gone, others UN; no cleanup needed

# 3. cass3 is dead: the survivors stream for it
nodetool status                  # DN ... <host ID of cass3>
nodetool removenode <host ID>    # on any live node
nodetool removenode status       # until no removals in process
nodetool repair -pr              # on every node, in case cass3 held the only copy of something
# or: start a new machine with -Dcassandra.replace_address_first_boot=<cass3's address>

recap: A node is one Java program plus `commitlog/`, `data/`, `hints/` and `saved_caches/`. Set the heap yourself, and get `cluster_name`, seeds, addresses, the snitch with `dc` and `rack`, `num_tokens` and the allocator right before the first start.

A joining node picks tokens, gossips them, sleeps 30 seconds and streams each new range from the replica it replaces. The old nodes keep their copies until `nodetool cleanup`, and nothing moves unless an operator starts it.
Decommission streams a live node's data away, removenode makes the survivors stream for a dead one, and `replace_address_first_boot` lets a new machine take a dead node's tokens.
Repair every node within `gc_grace_seconds` (incremental often, full every 1 to 3 weeks), drain before every restart, one node at a time, and copy snapshots off the node.
A new datacenter starts with `auto_bootstrap: false`, gets replicas with `ALTER KEYSPACE`, and serves clients only after `nodetool rebuild`, or reads at `LOCAL_*` come back empty.

The limit: in 5.0.9, every change is a step a person runs, and a join trusts gossip and a 30-second sleep. 6.0 (alpha) puts membership, tokens and schema in one log ordered by consensus, so every node applies a join in the same order.
closing:
We started with an office that ran out of cabinet space, because nobody told the old clerks to shred. A Cassandra join works the same way: the new node streams each range from the replica it replaces, and the old copies stay until `nodetool cleanup`. Repair, drain and snapshots are the same kind of job. Nothing does them unless someone schedules them.

If you run anything on a schedule, even a backup of your laptop, check when it last finished. A job that fails quietly hurts later.

Next, we'll leave Cassandra for MongoDB, which moves data between machines by itself, and find out why splitting payments by time sends every new one to the same machine.

quiz.q: In Cassandra 5.0, a joining node gossips its tokens and then sleeps 30 seconds before it streams. What does the sleep cover up, and what does 6.0's cluster metadata log do instead?
options: The Java program needs time to warm up; 6.0 starts faster

Gossip has no order and no confirmation, so the sleep is a guess that every node has heard of the new tokens; in 6.0 the join is a series of numbered entries in one log, which every node applies in the same order
Hints for the new node must be replayed first; 6.0 removes hints
A repair has to finish first; 6.0 repairs during the join
quiz.why: Gossip spreads the BOOT state in a few rounds but never confirms that everyone has it, so the join waits `ring_delay` and hopes. Transactional Cluster Metadata turns each step of the join into a log entry that the Cluster Metadata Service orders by consensus, so no node can act on a ring the others haven't reached. Hints and repair have nothing to do with the wait.

quiz.q: cass3's disk failed, and the node will never come back. Which command takes it off the ring properly?
options: `nodetool decommission` on cass3
`nodetool cleanup` on the other nodes
`nodetool removenode <cass3's host ID>` on a live node, then repair
Nothing: Cassandra drops dead nodes after `max_hint_window`
quiz.why: Decommission has to run on the leaving node, which streams its own data, and cass3 can't run anything, so the tempting first option fails. Removenode makes the surviving replicas stream to the new owners. Cassandra never takes a node off the ring by itself; after `max_hint_window` it only stops keeping hints for it.

quiz.q: `gc_grace_seconds` is the default 10 days on every table. Which repair schedule keeps deleted payments from coming back?
options: Incremental repair every 1 to 3 days and a full repair every week or two, with every node covered at least every 7 days
A full repair once a month, during the quietest week
Repair only on nodes that were down longer than 3 hours
No repair is needed when every write uses QUORUM
quiz.why: A replica that missed a delete has to receive its tombstone before the other copies may throw it away, after 10 days. So every node has to be repaired inside that window, with room to spare, and a monthly repair is far too late. QUORUM doesn't put the tombstone on every replica, and hints only cover 3 hours of downtime.

quiz.q: You added dc2 to the payments keyspace and pointed the apps in region 2 at dc2 with LOCAL_QUORUM, but forgot `nodetool rebuild`. What do they see?
options: Errors, because dc2 has no replicas yet
Correct data, read from dc1 across the regions
Correct data after a few seconds, once hints arrive
Missing or old rows: LOCAL_QUORUM asks only dc2's replicas, which hold only what was written since the ALTER
quiz.why: After the ALTER, dc2's nodes are replicas and receive new writes, so the consistency level is met and nothing fails, but they never got the older data. The Try it's LOCAL_ONE read returned 0 rows. Only `rebuild` (or a full repair) copies the existing data, and reads at LOCAL_* never fall back to dc1, so the second option fails.

quiz.q: From Wide-column stores with Cassandra: why does `nodetool drain` before a restart make the node come back faster?
options: It merges every SSTable into one
It flushes every memtable to an SSTable, so the commit log has nothing to replay at startup
It saves the row cache to disk
It skips the commit log for writes during the restart
quiz.why: A write is confirmed once it's in the commit log and the memtable. After a plain stop, the restart replays the commit log to rebuild the memtables it lost. Drain flushes them first, so there's nothing to replay: `0 replayed mutations` in the Try it. Drain also announces the shutdown, so peers mark the node down at once.

flashcards.front: What does Cassandra 6.0's Transactional Cluster Metadata change?
flashcards.back: Membership, tokens and schema move from gossip into one log ordered by the Cluster Metadata Service. Each change is an epoch, and a join is a series of logged steps every node applies in order.

flashcards.front: Which settings must be right before a node's first start?
flashcards.back: `cluster_name`, the snitch with `dc` and `rack`, `num_tokens` and `allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor`. They can't be changed in place later.

flashcards.front: Where does a joining node stream each range from?
flashcards.back: From the replica it replaces: the node that held the range before and doesn't after (`cassandra.consistent.rangemovement`, true by default).

flashcards.front: What does `nodetool cleanup` do, and when?
flashcards.back: It rewrites a node's SSTables without the ranges it no longer holds. Run it on each old node after the last new node is UN, one at a time.
decommission: the node is alive and leaving. removenode: the node is dead, and the survivors stream. `replace_address_first_boot`: a new machine takes a dead node's tokens.

flashcards.front: How often to repair with the default `gc_grace_seconds`?
flashcards.back: Incremental every 1 to 3 days, full every 1 to 3 weeks, every node at least every 7 days. `-pr` on every node avoids repairing each range three times.

flashcards.front: What is a snapshot, on disk?
flashcards.back: Hard links to the table's SSTables in `snapshots/<tag>/`, plus `schema.cql` and a manifest: no copy, and no extra space until compaction deletes the originals.

terms.plain: A new node's first join: choose tokens, announce them, then stream its ranges from the current owners before serving reads.
Copying the data of token ranges from node to node, during joins, removals, rebuilds and repairs.
`nodetool cleanup`: a compaction that drops the data for ranges a node no longer holds.
Retiring a live node: it streams its ranges to the new owners, then leaves the ring.
Taking a dead node off the ring; the remaining replicas stream its ranges to the new owners.
`nodetool repair`: comparing the copies of each range with Merkle trees and streaming what differs, so every replica holds the same data.
`nodetool drain`: stop client traffic, announce the shutdown and flush all memtables before a restart.
In Cassandra 6.0, the few nodes that put every change to membership, tokens and schema into one log, by consensus; each entry is an epoch.

explain_back.prompt: Your manager asks: "We need more room before the busy season. What exactly happens when we add a Cassandra node, how long will it take, and what do we have to do afterwards?" Answer in a few sentences.
explain_back.answer: We start the new node with the same cluster name and seeds and its rack set, and it isn't a seed itself, so it bootstraps. It learns the ring from a seed, picks 16 tokens with the allocator so the load stays even, and announces them; from then on it gets a copy of every new write for its future ranges. After 30 seconds it streams each of its ranges from the replica it's replacing. That's the long part: at the default 24 MiB/s per sender, about 400 GB takes over an hour and a half per node, so for three nodes we plan most of a day, adding one at a time and waiting for each to show UN. Afterwards we run `nodetool cleanup` on every old node, one at a time, because Cassandra doesn't delete the data they handed over, and without it their disks stay full. Then a repair, a check that every node owns about the same share, and an update to the runbook. None of it needs downtime: with three copies and LOCAL_QUORUM, payments keep flowing throughout.

deeper.body:
Two datacenters: the coordinator sends one copy of each write to a single node in the other datacenter, and that node passes it to the other replicas there, so the slow link between regions carries each write once. On a single node, the commit log's `batch` and `group` modes wait for the fsync before confirming a write, and pay for that safety in time.

Installing: Cassandra comes as a packed folder (`bin/`, `conf/`, `lib/`), as Linux packages, or as the Docker image the labs use, and its shell, `cqlsh`, needs Python 3. A node saves `cluster_name` on its first start and refuses to start if the file says something else later.

Disks: the commit log is written in order and forced to disk, while SSTables are read at random places. On spinning disks the two needed separate disks. On SSDs one volume works, but the commit log still competes with compaction for the disk's bandwidth. `data_file_directories` can list several disks, and Cassandra splits the token ranges between them.

A cluster upgraded from 5.0 to 6.0 keeps its gossip-held map until every node runs 6.0 and an operator runs `nodetool cms initialize`. 6.0 also brings Accord, transactions across partitions that a table opts into, which the Transactions track runs.

Addresses behind NAT, where a machine's own address differs from the one others reach it by: `broadcast_address` is what other nodes are told, next to `broadcast_rpc_address` for clients.

Streaming has two modes. When an SSTable lies entirely inside the ranges being moved, Cassandra 4.0 and later can send the whole file without decoding it (zero-copy, entire-SSTable streaming, limited by `entire_sstable_stream_throughput_outbound`). With 16 tokens per node, a joining node's ranges are small slices of every SSTable, so most streaming decodes each SSTable and sends only the partitions in range, limited by `stream_throughput_outbound`, 24 MiB/s by default. `nodetool setstreamthroughput` changes the limit on a running node: raise it for a planned expansion at night, lower it if streaming slows the clients down.

`nodetool netstats` shows streams in progress, per peer and per file, during a bootstrap, decommission, rebuild or repair. On the lab's tiny data set they finished between two calls, but on real clusters it's the command you watch. `nodetool removenode status` and `nodetool decommission` (which blocks until done) are the others.

Incremental repair splits SSTables into repaired and unrepaired sets, and compaction keeps the two apart, which is how `Percent repaired` in `tablestats` is measured. A full repair ignores the split. `nodetool tpstats` counts dropped messages: in an earlier, faster run of the ledger load, cass1 dropped 87,398 `MUTATION_REQ` messages, writes that waited past the write timeout, which hints and repair later put back. Tools such as Cassandra Reaper schedule repairs in small slices of the ring across the cluster, so that no single run takes hours. Whatever runs it, alert when a node hasn't completed a repair within 7 days.

`nodetool assassinate` exists, and its help text says what it is: it removes a dead node by force without copying any data again, as a last resort when `removenode` can't work. Data that lived only on that node is gone.

For restores, `nodetool import` loads SSTables you've copied into a table's folder on a live node, and `sstableloader` streams them to whichever nodes own them now, so it works even when the ring has changed since the snapshot. Restoring a whole cluster from snapshots is easiest when the new cluster has the same tokens: put each old node's tokens in the new node's `initial_token` before its first start.
